topic: The Effective Executive — Effectiveness Can Be Learned
subtopic: Effectiveness is a learnable discipline of practices, not a talent you are born with
content: No executive is born effective. Drucker, after decades of consulting across businesses, government, hospitals and universities, never met a single "natural" — every effective person had to learn the practices and drill them until they became habit, the way a pianist practises scales. The book's subject is managing oneself for effectiveness; whether one can truly manage other people is unproven, but one can always manage oneself, and executives who do not manage themselves for effectiveness cannot expect to manage their associates. Management is largely by example. Effectiveness is not intelligence, hard work or knowledge: brilliant people often fail because their insights never become disciplined work, while plodding people put one foot in front of the other and get there first. Intelligence, imagination and knowledge are essential resources, but only effectiveness converts them into results. Effectiveness is what executives are paid for, and it consists of a small number of simple practices that are deceptively hard to do well — they must be repeated until they become unthinking, conditioned reflex. The five practices: know where your time actually goes; focus outward on contribution and results; build on strengths; concentrate on the few areas that produce outstanding results, doing first things first and second things not at all; and make effective decisions systematically. Do not wait to feel ready; competence, not mastery, is what is needed — "the scales." She started writing one contribution goal each morning — a specific margin target — and checking it at close. Her weekly profit rose roughly 20% within a month, with no extra working hours.

topic: The Effective Executive — Knowledge Workers and Executive Effectiveness
subtopic: Anyone whose decisions affect results is an executive, paid for effectiveness, not activity
content: Knowledge work changed what it means to be an executive. Manual work needs only efficiency — doing things right against a definable output; it can be supervised, measured and told what to do. Knowledge work cannot be measured or closely supervised: the knowledge worker must direct himself toward performance and contribution. His specific work is thinking — the office of "Chas. Smith, General Sales Manager" proves you can never be sure the knowledge worker is thinking soap, yet thinking is his doing. If he cannot be effective, his commitment to work and contribution soon withers and he becomes a time-server going through the motions. A knowledge worker does not produce a physical product; he produces knowledge, ideas and information that are useless by themselves — somebody else must convert them into results, or the greatest wisdom is meaningless data. An executive is anyone who, by position or knowledge, is responsible for a contribution that materially affects the capacity of the organization to perform: the chemist who chooses one line of inquiry, the junior who decides what counts as a product in the books. Being a manager of people is not the test — the market-research man with two hundred staff may contribute less than the lone researcher. In guerrilla war every man is an executive, because each must judge the situation on the spot. For the small trader this is liberating: you are paid for decisions that turn knowledge into money — what to stock, how to price, whom to serve — and no one can supervise that for you. Protect your effectiveness — it is your real product.

By checking the TZS/UGX rate before each purchase he protected his margin on one shipment that would otherwise have lost about 8% to a weak shilling.

topic: The Effective Executive — The Eight Practices of Effective Executives
subtopic: The introduction's checklist: ask the right questions, plan, own decisions, communicate, seize opportunity, run meetings, say 'we'
content: Effective executives do not need to be leaders in the popular sense: Harry Truman had no charisma and some of the best CEOs Drucker worked with over 65 years were not stereotypical leaders. They ranged from extroverted to reclusive, easygoing to controlling, generous to parsimonious — what made them all effective was that they followed the same eight practices. The first two give knowledge: ask "What needs to be done?" and "What is right for the enterprise?" The next four convert knowledge into action: develop action plans; take responsibility for decisions; take responsibility for communicating; and focus on opportunities rather than problems. The last two ensure the whole organization feels responsible and accountable: run productive meetings, and think and say "we" rather than "I." The two knowledge practices supply direction; the four action practices translate insight into deeds; the final two build shared accountability across the enterprise. Drucker then adds a bonus practice he elevates to the level of a rule: listen first, speak last. Effective executives differ widely in personality, strengths, weaknesses, values and beliefs — all they have in common is that they get the right things done. The demand is much too great to be satisfied by extraordinary talent: effectiveness is a discipline, and like every discipline it can be learned and must be earned. Within two quarters he had stopped attending meetings he did not need, named owners for every restock decision, and put opportunities — not complaints — at the top of his Sunday review. Stock-outs fell by a third and his two assistants began proposing opportunities unprompted.

topic: The Effective Executive — Ask 'What Needs to Be Done?'
subtopic: Not 'what do I want to do?' — concentrate on the task the situation demands
content: The first practice is to ask "What needs to be done?" — note that it is not "What do I want to do?" Asking what has to be done, and taking the question seriously, is crucial for managerial success; failure to ask renders even the ablest executive ineffectual. Truman became president knowing exactly what he wanted — completing the economic and social reforms of the New Deal deferred by the war — but as soon as he asked what needed to be done, foreign affairs had absolute priority. He organized his days to begin with foreign-policy tutorials and became the most effective president in foreign affairs the United States has known. Welch realized at GE that what needed doing was not the overseas expansion he wanted but getting rid of businesses that could not be number one or number two in their industries. The answer almost always contains more than one urgent task, but effective executives do not splinter themselves: they concentrate on one task, or two for the sizable minority who work best with a change of pace — Drucker never met an executive who remained effective tackling more than two at a time. So after asking the question, they set priorities and stick to them; other tasks, no matter how appealing, are postponed. After completing the top priority they reset priorities rather than moving down the original list, asking again "What must be done now?" — Welch re-asked every five years and each time arrived at a new priority. Finally, ask which of the top tasks you yourself are best suited to do; concentrate on that and delegate the rest. He gave the launch to his trained assistant and concentrated on two core suppliers for a quarter. On-time deliveries rose from 65% to 90% and margins recovered before he reopened the expansion plan.

topic: The Effective Executive — What Is Right for the Enterprise?
subtopic: Decide for the good of the enterprise, not for owners, share price or favourites
content: The second practice — fully as important as the first — is to ask "Is this the right thing for the enterprise?" Effective executives do not ask if a decision is right for the owners, the stock price, the employees or the executives. They know shareholders, employees and executives are important constituencies who must support a decision, or at least acquiesce in it, for it to be effective, and that the share price matters because the price/earnings ratio sets the cost of capital. But they also know a decision that is not right for the enterprise will ultimately not be right for any stakeholder. This practice matters especially in family-owned and family-run businesses — the majority of businesses in every country — particularly in decisions about people. In the successful family company, a relative is promoted only if he or she is measurably superior to all nonrelatives at the same level. At DuPont, all top managers except the controller and lawyer were family members in the early years, and every male descendant was entitled to an entry-level job; but beyond the entrance level, a family member got a promotion only when a panel composed primarily of nonfamily managers judged the person superior in ability and performance to all other employees at the same level. The same rule held for a century in J. Lyons & Company while it dominated British food service and hotels. Asking the question does not guarantee the right decision — even the most brilliant executive is human and prone to prejudice — but failure to ask virtually guarantees the wrong one. Following the DuPont rule, he posted the promotion criteria and let two senior non-family staff score the candidates. The cousin came third, the best-performing buyer was promoted, and monthly procurement losses dropped by a fifth.

topic: The Effective Executive — Action Plans
subtopic: Plans as intentions, revised often, with check-ins and control of your time
content: Executives are doers; knowledge is useless until translated into deeds. But before springing into action, the executive plans: think about desired results, probable restraints, future revisions, check-in points, and the implications for how time will be spent. First, define desired results by asking what contributions the enterprise should expect from you over the next 18 months to two years, what results you will commit to, and with what deadlines. Then consider the restraints on action: Is the course ethical? Is it acceptable within the organization? Is it legal? Is it compatible with the mission, values and policies of the organization? Affirmative answers do not guarantee the action will be effective, but violating these restraints is certain to make it both wrong and ineffectual. The action plan is a statement of intentions rather than a commitment; it must not become a straitjacket. Revise it often, because every success creates new opportunities and so does every failure, as do changes in the business environment, the market and people — a written plan should anticipate the need for flexibility. Build in a system for checking results against expectations: usually two checks — one halfway through the plan's period (say, at nine months) and one at the end, before the next plan is drawn up. Finally, the action plan must become the basis for your time management; organizations are inherently time wasters, and a plan is useless unless it determines how you spend your time. Napoleon allegedly said no successful battle ever followed its plan — yet he planned every battle more meticulously than earlier generals. Without a plan the executive becomes a prisoner of events; without check-ins he cannot know which events matter and which are only noise. She hit the 22% margin in month five instead of drifting to a disappointed year-end.

topic: The Effective Executive — Take Responsibility for Decisions
subtopic: A decision is unmade until an owner, a deadline, the affected and the informed are named
content: A decision has not been made until people know the name of the person accountable for carrying it out; the deadline; the names of the people who will be affected and therefore have to know about, understand and approve it — or at least not be strongly opposed to it; and the names of the people who have to be informed even if they are not directly affected. An extraordinary number of decisions run into trouble because these bases are not covered: one of Drucker's clients lost its leadership position in the fast-growing Japanese market because nobody was ever told to inform the purchasing agents that the new partner defined specifications in meters and kilograms rather than feet and pounds. Review decisions periodically at a time agreed on in advance — covering anything from results to the assumptions underlying the decision — so a poor decision can be corrected before real damage. This review matters most for the most crucial and difficult of all decisions, those about hiring or promoting people: studies show only one-third of such choices turn out truly successful, one-third draws, one-third failures. Effective executives check six to nine months later; if a decision has not produced the desired results they conclude that they themselves made a mistake, not that the person failed. They do not tolerate nonperformers in important jobs, but people who fail after a promotion should be offered a return to their former level — an option rarely exercised, yet one that powerfully encourages people to take risky new assignments. Decision review is also a tool for self-development: it reveals your strengths, your biases, and the areas in which you are simply incompetent — and in those areas smart executives delegate. Integrate: convert every decision into a named task with an owner and deadline in BirichiNex Orders or Routines, and set the six-to-nine-month review date in Analytics.

When payments fell behind, he re-ran the decision properly: the cashier owns the ledger, the owner approves limits, and a reminder message goes to every customer on the due date. Within a quarter late payments dropped by half.

topic: The Effective Executive — Take Responsibility for Communicating
subtopic: Share your plans and push for the information you need; information holds the enterprise together
content: Effective executives make sure that both their action plans and their information needs are understood. They share their plans with and ask for comments from all their colleagues — superiors, subordinates and peers — and at the same time let each person know what information they will need to get the job done. The information flow from subordinate to boss usually gets the most attention, but executives need to give equal attention to the information needs of peers and superiors. Thanks to Chester Barnard's 1938 classic The Functions of the Executive, we know organizations are held together by information rather than by ownership or command. Yet far too many executives behave as if information and its flow were the job of the information specialist — for example, the accountant — with the result that they get an enormous amount of data they do not need and cannot use, but little of the information they do need. The best way around this problem: each executive identifies the information he needs, asks for it, and keeps pushing until he gets it. The reports and numbers only become useful when someone takes responsibility for turning them into decisions. For the small business, this is the difference between the owner who passively receives whatever stock, sales and cash figures happen to be collected and the owner who specifies exactly which figures matter, in which form, and by when — then insists on receiving them. topic: The Effective Executive — Focus on Opportunities
subtopic: Problems prevent damage; opportunities produce results — staff your best people on the future
content: Good executives focus on opportunities rather than problems. Problems have to be taken care of — they must not be swept under the rug — but problem solving, however necessary, does not produce results; it prevents damage. Exploiting opportunities produces results. Above all, effective executives treat change as an opportunity rather than a threat, and systematically scan seven situations for opportunities: an unexpected success or failure in their own enterprise, a competing enterprise, or the industry; a gap between what is and what could be in a market, process, product or service (in the nineteenth century, the paper industry concentrated on the 10% of each tree that became wood pulp and neglected the possibilities in the remaining 90% that became waste); innovation in a process, product or service, inside or outside the enterprise; changes in industry structure and market structure; demographics; changes in mind-set, values, perception, mood or meaning; and new knowledge or a new technology. Executives also make sure problems do not overwhelm opportunities: list opportunities on the first page of the monthly report and problems on the second; unless there is a true catastrophe, problems are not discussed in management meetings until opportunities have been analyzed and dealt with. Staffing is another aspect of being opportunity-focused: put your best people on opportunities rather than problems. One method is to ask each member of the management group to prepare two lists every six months — one of opportunities for the enterprise and one of the best-performing people — then meld them into two master lists and match the best people with the best opportunities; in Japan this matching is considered a major HR task. Integrate: BirichiNex Analytics can surface opportunities — fast-moving lines, repeat customers, restock gaps — and the entrepreneur hub can hold your six-monthly best-people-to-best-opportunities matching.

topic: The Effective Executive — Meeting Types and Follow-Up
subtopic: Decide in advance what kind of meeting it is; end when the purpose is met; memo the follow-up
content: Studies of the executive workday find that even junior executives and professionals are with other people — in a meeting of some sort — more than half of every working day; even a conversation with one other person is a meeting. So executives must make meetings productive work sessions rather than bull sessions. The key: decide in advance what kind of meeting it will be, because different kinds need different preparation and different results. A meeting to prepare a statement, announcement or press release requires one member to prepare a draft beforehand and a preappointed member to take responsibility for disseminating the final text. A meeting to make an announcement should be confined to the announcement and a discussion about it. A meeting in which one member reports should discuss nothing but the report. A meeting in which several or all members report should have either no discussion or only clarifying questions, with reports distributed well beforehand and each capped at a set time such as fifteen minutes. A meeting to inform the convening executive: the executive listens and asks questions, sums up, but does not present. Finally, the meeting whose only function is to let participants be in the executive's presence — the penalty of rank — can never be made productive; effective executives confine such meetings to breakfast and dinner. It also takes self-discipline to terminate a meeting as soon as its purpose is accomplished: effective executives do not raise another matter for discussion; they sum up and adjourn. Follow-up is as important as the meeting itself. Sloan, who spent most of six working days a week in meetings, announced the purpose at the start, listened, summed up — then immediately wrote a short memo to one attendee summarizing the discussion and conclusions, spelling out each work assignment, its deadline and the accountable executive, and copying everyone present. topic: The Effective Executive — Think and Say 'We'
subtopic: Ultimate responsibility is yours alone; think of the enterprise before yourself, listen first, speak last
content: The final practice is simple to state and hard to observe: do not think or say "I" — think and say "we." Effective executives know that they have ultimate responsibility, which can be neither shared nor delegated, but that they hold authority only because they have the trust of the organization. This means they think of the needs and opportunities of the organization before they think of their own needs and opportunities. Drucker adds a bonus practice he elevates to the level of a rule: listen first, speak last. The effective executives he observed differed widely in their personalities, strengths, weaknesses, values and beliefs — but all they have in common is that they get the right things done. And because the demand for effectiveness is much too great to be satisfied by extraordinary talent, it must be treated as a discipline: like every discipline, effectiveness can be learned and must be earned. For a shop owner this shows up in small daily habits: speaking of "our stock, our customers, our name" with staff, suppliers and the mobile-money agent; holding back your own opinion in a negotiation until the other side has fully stated its position; and taking personal responsibility for results rather than blaming staff, government, customers or "the market." The "we" is not self-effacement — it is the recognition that your results depend on people you do not control, and your authority depends on their trust. topic: The Effective Executive — The Four Realities of the Executive
subtopic: Time belongs to others, events force you to operate, you need sideways allies, and you are insulated from results
content: The realities of the executive's situation both demand effectiveness and make it exceedingly difficult; unless executives work at becoming effective, these realities push them into futility. There are four, and the executive has essentially no control over any of them — his only choice is to cooperate with the inevitable. First, the executive's time tends to belong to everybody else: operationally, an executive is a captive of the organization, and everyone moves in on his time; Carlson's study found even the most effective executives had most of their time taken up by the demands of others. Second, the executive is forced to keep on "operating" unless he takes positive action to change the reality he lives in — the flow of events determines what he works on, and unlike the doctor, whose patient's complaint establishes the priorities, events never tell the executive what is important; they are not even symptoms. Third, the executive is within an organization, and is effective only if and when other people make use of what he contributes; the people most important to his effectiveness are usually sideways or above — people over whom he has no direct control. Fourth, he sees the inside as close and immediate reality and the outside only through thick, distorting lenses of reports, and the higher he rises the more inside-focused he becomes. These four realities cannot be changed, but they can be fought: deliberately refusing to let events run the day, cultivating sideways and upward relationships, and making special conscious efforts to perceive the outside. He set a 9am rule: process partner requests before internal chatter. Supplier complaints dropped and one broker offered priority loading, cutting dispatch time by a day.

topic: The Effective Executive — Results Are Outside the Organization
subtopic: Inside is effort and cost; the important outside events are qualitative and cannot be counted
content: There are no results within the organization — all results are on the outside. A business's only results come from a customer who converts the costs and efforts of the business into revenues and profits through his willingness to exchange purchasing power for its products. What happens inside any organization is effort and cost; to speak of "profit centers" is polite euphemism — there are only effort centers. The less an organization has to do to produce results, the better it does its job. Yet the inside is what is most visible and immediate to the executive, and the bigger and more successful an organization gets, the more inside events engage his energies to the exclusion of his real effectiveness in the outside. The computer aggravates the danger: it can handle only quantifiable data, and one can by and large quantify only what goes on inside — costs, production figures, statistics. The relevant outside events are often qualitative and not yet "facts": the thalidomide tragedy was caught in the United States because one public-health physician perceived a qualitative change — a minor, by itself meaningless, skin tingling — and related it to an earlier event, sounding the alarm before the drug was used, while the statistics arrived too late to help in Europe. The Ford Edsel gathered every quantitative figure that could possibly be obtained, all pointing to the right car for the right market; the qualitative change — buying shifting from income-determined to taste-determined market segmentation — could not be shown statistically, and by the time it could be captured in numbers the Edsel had failed. The important outside events are not trends but changes in trends, and these have to be perceived, not counted. Guard against "computeritis" and make conscious efforts to gain direct access to outside reality. topic: The Effective Executive — The Promise of Effectiveness
subtopic: Universal genius is scarce; effectiveness is the tool that makes abilities yield more
content: Increasing effectiveness may well be the only area where we can hope significantly to raise the level of executive performance, achievement and satisfaction. We could use people of greater abilities and broader knowledge, but expecting too much from further efforts in these two areas is unprofitable — we are not going to breed a new race of supermen, and we will have to run our organizations with men as they are. The books on manager development envisage a true "man for all seasons": the manager of tomorrow is to be an analyst, a decision-maker, good with people, good at mathematics, possessed of artistic insight and creative imagination. What is wanted is universal genius, and universal genius has always been in scarce supply; the experience of the human race indicates strongly that the only person in abundant supply is the universal incompetent. We will therefore have to staff our organizations with people who at best excel in one of these abilities and are more than likely to lack any but the most modest endowment in the others — and we must learn to build organizations so that any man with strength in one important area is capable of putting it to work. The operations-research prescriptions that demanded a polymath with advanced knowledge in sixty-two major disciplines illustrate the same error: such a man, if found, would be totally wasted on inventory studies. If one cannot increase the supply of a resource, one must increase its yield — and effectiveness is the one tool that makes the resources of ability and knowledge yield more and better results. topic: The Effective Executive — Recording the Time Log
subtopic: Know where your time actually goes before you try to manage it
content: Drucker's first step to effectiveness is not planning — it is recording where your time goes. Discussions of the executive's task usually start with the advice to plan one's work; it sounds plausible, but it rarely works because the plans always remain on paper as good intentions. Effective executives start by finding out where their time actually goes, then manage it, then consolidate it into large continuing units. The foundation is that time is the limiting factor, and memory cannot be trusted: people kept in a room without light or darkness rapidly lose all sense of time, and even with lights on most people cannot estimate elapsed time. When Drucker asks executives to write down their guess and then run an actual record, there is never much resemblance between the two. One company chairman was certain he spent a third of his time with senior men, a third with important customers, a third on community activities; the record over six weeks showed he spent almost no time in any of these areas — he spent most of his hours as a dispatcher, tracking orders from customers he personally knew and bothering the plant with telephone calls about them. The effective executive therefore knows that to manage his time he must first know where it actually goes. The record must be made in real time, at the moment of the event, not later from memory; a secretary can do it for you. Effective executives keep a continuous log and review it monthly, or at minimum run it for three to four weeks twice a year on a regular schedule. After each sample they rethink and rework their schedule — and six months later they invariably find they have drifted back into trivia, which is exactly why the log is a continuing discipline, not a one-off exercise. Integrate: log your day against the tasks in BirichiNex Routines and let Analytics reveal how much time busywork such as reconciliation and reordering really consumes.

topic: The Effective Executive — Time Is the Unique Resource
subtopic: Inelastic, perishable, irreplaceable — the scarcest resource sets the limit of accomplishment
content: Effective executives know that time is the limiting factor: the output limits of any process are set by its scarcest resource, and in the process we call accomplishment, that resource is time. Of the other major resources, money is actually quite plentiful — it is the demand for capital, rather than its supply, that sets the limit to economic growth and activity. People — the third limiting resource — one can hire, though one can rarely hire enough good people. But one cannot rent, hire, buy or otherwise obtain more time. Its supply is totally inelastic: no matter how high the demand, the supply will not go up; there is no price for it and no marginal utility curve. Moreover, time is totally perishable and cannot be stored — yesterday's time is gone forever and will never come back, so time is always in exceedingly short supply. Time is totally irreplaceable: within limits we can substitute one resource for another, copper for aluminum, capital for human labor, more knowledge for more brawn — but there is no substitute for time. Everything requires time; it is the one truly universal condition. All work takes place in time and uses up time. Yet most people take this unique, irreplaceable and necessary resource for granted — and nothing else, perhaps, distinguishes effective executives as much as their tender loving care of time. Man is also ill-equipped to manage time, having no reliable time sense, which is why memory cannot be trusted and the time log must be kept in real time. The practical chain of consequences: because time cannot be bought, the only way to have more is to find out where it goes, cut the waste, and consolidate the remainder into large chunks. topic: The Effective Executive — Managing Time
subtopic: Three diagnostic questions to cut unproductive demands from your day
content: Once the time log exists, the second step is to manage time: find the nonproductive, time-wasting activities and get rid of them. Three diagnostic questions do this. First: "What would happen if this were not done at all?" If the answer is nothing, stop doing it. The dinner-eating chief executive found a third of his official dinners would proceed just as well without senior management — in fact his hosts had expected to be turned down. Drucker has yet to see an executive who could not consign about a quarter of the demands on his time to the wastepaper basket without anybody's noticing. Second: "Which of these activities could somebody else do just as well, if not better?" The usual sermon about delegation makes little sense — you are paid to do your own work, and the laziest-manager-is-best idea is nonsense. But every executive confronted with his time record rapidly acquires the habit of pushing onto others everything he need not do personally: a junior can take the trip (travel is still a novelty to him and he sleeps better in hotel beds), attend the meeting, chase the supplier. The point is not to delegate for its own sake but to get really to your own work. Third: "What do I do that wastes other people's time?" Ask directly and without coyness. One senior financial executive called every subordinate to every meeting for fear the uninvited would feel slighted; when he finally asked, they considered the meetings a waste and were relieved when he switched to a printed note — "come if you think you need the information, you will receive a full summary" — that cut a dozen people and a whole afternoon to three people and about an hour. Executives are afraid to prune, fearing they will cut out something important; but the mistake is quickly corrected, and we tend to overrate rather than underrate our own importance. topic: The Effective Executive — Pruning the Time-Wasters
subtopic: Recurrent crises, overstaffing, too many meetings and malfunctioning information are management diseases
content: Beyond personal habits, time is wasted by poor management and deficient organization — and poor management wastes everybody's time, above all the manager's. Four causes dominate. First, the recurrent crisis, which is the symptom to watch for: a crisis that recurs a second time must not occur again. It should always have been foreseen and converted into a routine — a routine makes unskilled people capable of doing what once took near-genius, because it sets down in systematic steps what a very able man learned in surmounting yesterday's crisis. The well-managed plant is a quiet, boring place; the "dramatic" organization is the poorly managed one, because heroics in mopping up yesterday replace basic decisions that make the future. A company's annual December earnings scramble disappeared with one stroke — predicting results within a range instead of a definite year-end figure; McNamara ended the defense establishment's May-June spending spree by using a legal interim account. Second, overstaffing: if senior people spend more than about a tenth of their time on feuds, frictions and questions of cooperation, the work force is too large — people get in each other's way. The "we have to have a thermodynamicist on the staff" specialist who is never used does nothing but mischief. Third, malorganization, whose symptom is an excess of meetings: one either meets or works; meetings are by definition a concession to deficient organization. A quarter of the time in meetings means malorganization, with responsibility diffused and information not going to those who need it. Fourth, malfunction in information: the hospital that turned away patients because beds were only counted at 5 a.m. while most discharges happened mid-morning — one extra carbon copy of the discharge chit fixed it — and reports that give accountants' averages when operators need the range and extremes. topic: The Effective Executive — Consolidating Discretionary Time
subtopic: Big tasks need big blocks; small dribbles of time are no time at all
content: After recording and pruning, the third step is to consolidate your discretionary time — the small share of your day genuinely under your control. Senior executives rarely have as much as a quarter of their time truly at their disposal, yet a quarter, gathered into large chunks, is usually enough to get the important things done; even three quarters of the day are useless as fifteen minutes here and half an hour there. Small driblets are no time at all: a report needs six or eight hours of first-draft time — fifteen minutes twice a day for three weeks leaves only blank paper. The method matters less than the approach. Some people work at home one day a week; others schedule all operating work for Monday and Friday and give Tuesday to Thursday mornings to major matters in ninety-minute blocks. The bank president Drucker observed had an hour-and-a-half attention span and held his meetings to it; his secretary put through nobody except the President and his wife, and he had yet to come across a crisis that could not wait ninety minutes. Most people make the mistake of pushing the secondary matters together to clear a free space, which keeps priority in the mind with trivia; instead, effective executives estimate how much discretionary time they can realistically call their own, set it aside first, and when other matters encroach they scrutinize the record again and cut more time-wasters — they know one rarely overprunes. They control their time management perpetually: keeping a continuing log and setting themselves deadlines for the important and the unpleasant tasks, with slippage as the alarm that time is getting away. Working at night after dinner is the weakest option — by then most people are too tired to do a good job, and taking work home lets an executive avoid tackling his time during the day. topic: The Effective Executive — People Decisions Take Large Blocks of Time
subtopic: People are time-consumers; fast personnel decisions are wrong decisions
content: Working with people is a central task of the executive, and people are time-consumers. A few minutes with someone is simply not productive — to get anything across you need at least an hour and usually much more; to establish a relationship, infinitely more. Knowledge workers make even greater time demands than manual workers because their work cannot be measured in simple units: you can tell a manual worker "fifty pieces an hour, you turned out forty-two," but with a knowledge worker you must sit down and think through what should be done and why before you can judge whether the job is satisfactory. Fast personnel decisions are likely to be wrong decisions. The good personnel decision needs an amazingly large quantum of time: what the decision involves often becomes clear only after one has gone around the same track several times. Sloan, the most effective business executive Drucker knew, never made a personnel decision the first time it came up — he made a tentative judgment after several hours, then tackled the question again days or weeks later as if he had never worked on it, and only went ahead when the same name came up two or three times in a row: "the first name I come up with is likely to be the wrong name." A research institute director solved an apparently impossible personnel problem only when he and his deputy sat down for a quiet evening of three or four uninterrupted hours — the "obvious" solution, moving a deteriorating senior man to a needed job he could still do, emerged simply because they finally gave it enough time. People are always "almost fits" at best; to get work done with people requires lots of time, thought and judgment. Integrate: schedule hiring and promotion decisions as ninety-minute blocks in BirichiNex Routines and re-review the shortlist on a later day before committing.

topic: The Effective Executive — Focus on Contribution
subtopic: Ask 'what can I contribute?' not 'what should I get?'
content: The effective executive looks up from the work and outward toward goals. Instead of asking what the organization owes them or what authority they should have, they ask: "What can I contribute that will significantly affect the performance and the results of the institution I serve?" The head of a management consulting firm opens each assignment by asking senior executives — rarely in these words — "And what do you do that justifies your being on the payroll?" The great majority answer "I run the accounting department," "I am in charge of the sales force," or "I have 850 people working under me." Only a few say "It's my job to give our managers the information they need to make the right decisions" or "I am responsible for finding out what products the customer will want tomorrow." The man who focuses on efforts and downward authority is a subordinate no matter how exalted his title; the man who focuses on contribution and takes responsibility for results is, in the most literal sense, top management. Focusing on contribution turns the executive away from his specialty and toward the outside, the only place where results exist. A government publications director whose work looked unpolished was writing for the young scientists and brought in recruits; his polished successor wrote at them and lost the audience. A bank's Agency department, a humdrum paper-pushing service, became a sales force for the whole bank when a new vice-president asked "What could Agency contribute?" Ask four things: what contribution does my business need from me, what can I alone do that done really well would make a difference, what information do I need and who needs my output, and what standards should I set myself? topic: The Effective Executive — The Three Kinds of Results
subtopic: Direct results, living values, and developing people for tomorrow
content: Every organization needs performance in three areas, and an executive's contribution must feed all three. First, direct results — the visible output: in a business, economic results such as sales and profits; in a hospital, patient care. These come first; like calories, without them the business starves. But they are not the whole diet. Second, a commitment to values and their constant reaffirmation — something "this organization stands for," like vitamins and minerals; without it the organization degenerates into disorganization, confusion and paralysis. A shop that passes off faded bales as first-grade may hit this month's numbers while destroying the trust that brings customers back. Values, like results, are not unambiguous: the British nationalized airlines, whipsawed between being run as a business, as an instrument of national policy, and to keep the aircraft industry alive, did poorly in respect to all three; the U.S. Department of Agriculture wavered for years between agricultural productivity and the "family farm," spending prodigious amounts of money while achieving neither. Third, developing people for tomorrow — an organization that cannot perpetuate itself has failed; it must renew its human capital and upgrade its human resources, so that the next generation stands on the shoulders of this one and sets a new high as the baseline. An organization that only perpetuates today's level has lost the capacity to adapt, and since the one certain thing is change, it will not survive a changed tomorrow. An executive's focus on contribution is itself a powerful force in developing people, because people adjust to the level of the demands made on them. A year later he opened a second stall staffed by the helper — sales up 60% across both, with the same quality reputation.

topic: The Effective Executive — Standards That Raise People (Nurse Bryan's Rule)
subtopic: People adjust to the level of demands made on them; one high standard raises everyone
content: People adjust to the level of the demands made on them — and a leader's focus on contribution raises the sights and standards of everyone he works with. Nurse Bryan was a long-serving nurse who never became a supervisor and was not particularly distinguished, but whenever a decision on patient care came up on her floor she would ask: "Are we doing the best we can do to help this patient?" Patients on her floor did better and recovered faster. Over the years the whole hospital adopted what came to be known as "Nurse Bryan's Rule" — asking "Are we really making the best contribution to the purpose of this hospital?" — and though she retired nearly ten years earlier, the standards she set still made demands on people who were her superiors in training and position. A new hospital administrator, thinking a rather difficult matter settled at his first staff meeting, had the argument reopened by one participant asking "Would this have satisfied Nurse Bryan?" — and it did not subside until a new and much more ambitious solution was hammered out. The same mechanism works both ways: people in general, and knowledge workers in particular, grow according to the demands they make on themselves. If they demand little of themselves, they remain stunted; if they demand a good deal, they grow to giant stature — without any more effort than the nonachievers expend. Set standards grounded in the requirements of the task rather than in personalities, and make them demands for excellence, high aspiration, ambitious goals and work of great impact. topic: The Effective Executive — Change with the New Position
subtopic: Keep doing what worked before and you fail; contribution shifts with the role
content: The most common cause of executive failure is the inability or unwillingness to change with the demands of a new position. The executive who keeps on doing what he has done successfully before he moved is almost bound to fail — not only do the results change to which his contribution ought to direct itself, but the relative importance of the three dimensions of performance changes. He will suddenly do the wrong things the wrong way, even though he does exactly what in his old job had been the right things done the right way. This was the main reason so many able men failed as executives in wartime Washington: the men who succeeded focused on contribution and changed both what they did and the weight they gave to each dimension; the failures often worked much harder but never challenged themselves or saw the need to redirect their efforts. A man who became chief executive of a nationwide retail chain after twenty years as the second-in-command asked himself: "What can I and no one else do which, if done really well, would make a real difference to this company?" His answer was the development of tomorrow's managers — so he walked through the personnel department three times a week, picked out ten folders of young supervisors, and phoned their managers to insist that promised development moves actually happened. McNamara, the perfect "inside" man at Ford, realized within weeks that as Secretary of Defense he depended on congressional understanding and support, and forced himself to master the strange art of congressional infighting although he was publicity-shy and nonpolitical. The higher the position, the larger the outside looms in the contribution. topic: The Effective Executive — Human Relations from Contribution
subtopic: Good relationships are productive ones — communication, teamwork, self-development and developing others
content: Executives do not have good human relations because they have a "talent for people"; they have good human relations because they focus on contribution in their work and relationships. Warm feelings and pleasant words are meaningless, and a false front for wretched attitudes, if there is no achievement in what is, after all, a work-focused relationship — while an occasional rough word will not disturb a relationship that produces results for all concerned. Drucker names Marshall, Sloan and Dreystadt as the three executives with the best human relations he knew — completely different personalities — all of whom built their relationships around contribution and took "good human relations" for granted. The focus on contribution supplies the four basic requirements of effective human relations: first, communications — communication downward does not work; superiors cannot get their message through to subordinates, who hear what they expect to hear, so ask instead "What contributions should we hold you accountable for?" and let subordinates state their own contribution; second, teamwork — asking "Who has to use my output for it to become effective?" reveals the people sideways to you, and effective work is done by teams of diverse knowledge organized around the task; third, self-development — asking "what is the most important contribution I can make?" forces the question of what knowledge and skill you must acquire; fourth, developing others — setting standards grounded in the requirements of the task makes demands for excellence, and people grow to the level of those demands. Integrate: in BirichiNex CRM, define each partner's and employee's expected contribution and hold the monthly review against it — communication, teamwork and development follow.

topic: The Effective Executive — The Effective Meeting
subtopic: Convening is a serious responsibility; decide the kind of meeting before you call it
content: Convening a meeting — large or small — is a serious and visible act of an executive's real job, and it is a mark of effectiveness to know which meetings are necessary, what the meeting is for, and what its expected outcome should be. Every effective meeting is sharply defined and strictly limited to one discussion: either it is a meeting to provide information and announce something — the "announcement meeting" — or a meeting to report or share information, in which everyone contributes; or a meeting in which people try to make a decision; or, very frequently, a meeting to impress, by which the executive uses the occasion to enhance his or her role or the role of the organization. The decision meeting is the one on which almost all effectiveness — or ineffectiveness — hangs, and the discipline is to control its content and its duration. The effective executive states the specific purpose and contribution of the meeting in advance: "We meet to give personnel the information they need so that their judgment on the promotion decisions will be sound," or "We meet to clarify what we should do to change our production schedule." He asks "What is this meeting for?" and cancels or reforms it if the answer is vague. He makes sure the meeting is followed by a summary of conclusions and assignments that spells out what was agreed, who is responsible, and by when — and he follows up. The effective executive distinguishes between the kinds of meetings and convenes only the ones the work requires: a one-way information meeting is efficient and can be short; a discussion meeting needs the right people and enough time; a decision meeting needs clear alternatives and a recommendation. topic: The Effective Executive — Making the Specialist Effective
subtopic: A specialty is a fragment; the specialist is effective only when connected to the whole
content: Knowledge workers are specialists; they are effective only because they learned to do one thing very well. But by itself a specialty is a fragment and is sterile: its output must be joined with the output of other specialists before it can produce results. The task is not to breed generalists but to enable the specialist to make himself and his specialty effective — which means he must think through who is to use his output, and what the user needs to know and understand to be able to make the fragment productive. The cost accountant, for example, may know that prices, margins and quality of output are the key figures, yet his reports are often in a form the operating manager cannot use; the biochemist must think through how his findings can be understood by the clinician who will act on them; the market researcher must state findings so that the production manager can act. Each must ask: "Who has to know about it? What does he have to know? How can he get it?" The man of knowledge has always been expected to take responsibility for being understood — it is barbarian arrogance to assume that the layman can make the effort. The specialist who asks these questions makes his fragment a tool the whole organization can use, and in the process often discovers that he has been doing the wrong things: figures the manager needs but never gets, assumptions of his own that are unfamiliar and misleading to others. Integrate: define the exact output your market needs — stock lists, price lists, delivery schedules — and deliver it through BirichiNex Orders, Procurement and CRM in the form buyers can actually use.

Asked what he needed, he wanted one page: cash in hand, what customers owe, what suppliers are owed. The bookkeeper changed the format — and the owner started acting on the numbers, catching a 10% margin leak in the first quarter.

topic: The Effective Executive — Staff from Strength
subtopic: Make strengths productive and weaknesses irrelevant; the 'well-rounded' man is mediocre
content: The first rule of staffing is to make strengths productive and weaknesses irrelevant — and to build on what a person can do rather than on what he cannot. An executive who tries to avoid weakness rather than make strength effective ends up, at best, with mediocrity. The "well-rounded" man does not exist: strong people always have strong weaknesses too, and where there are peaks there are valleys. Lincoln's great strength was his ability to select and use the men he worked with — he chose each general for one great strength, and he held in his cabinet a man like Seward because he was brilliant, not because he was congenial. Andrew Carnegie's own tombstone reads: "Here lies a man who knew how to bring into his service men better than he was." The effective executive does not ask "Is this man good?" — the question is "What can he do uncommonly well?" He looks first for one area of excellence, not several, and he accepts that this strength comes attached to a whole personality: the prima donna in the opera house is often impossible to live with and equally impossible to do without, so the general manager soothes her ego and secures her performances. This is not softness; it is deliberate. The organization exists to make strengths effective and weaknesses irrelevant, and every position is a demand for one or two strengths, not for all-round excellence. Staffing is the one act in which the executive has no second chance — the decision cannot be undone easily — so it deserves the deepest care. Integrate: staff every BirichiNex role from the one strength the role demands — inventory, finance, CRM, orders — and design the routine so the person's weakness never touches the task.
tips: Hire for one area of excellence, not for an absence of faults.
Ask 'what can this person do uncommonly well?' before anything else.
Do not hire to avoid weakness — that is how you get mediocrity.
Tolerate the strength's shadow: the prima donna comes with the voice.
Match people to positions, not positions to your comfort.
Make the person's weakness irrelevant by design, not by hope.
examples: A Mombasa shop owner tried to make his best seller do the books because he was reliable — and the books suffered. He split the roles: the seller sells, a meticulous cousin does accounts. Sales rose 15% in two months and reconciliation errors vanished.

topic: The Effective Executive — Jobs Must Be Objective, Not Fitted to People
subtopic: Never tailor a job to a person; the job must exist before the person
content: Jobs must be objective, determined by the task rather than by the personality available to fill them — this is the second rule of staffing. The temptation is to structure a job around a particular person: the employer who tells his assistant, "Look, I'll just make you my sales manager, and you can decide what you want to sell and how," may be creating a job for a favorite employee, but the job will not work, because a job is not something to be invented for a person; it is the work to be done, and it must be defined before anyone is chosen to do it. The effective executive defines the job in terms of its contribution — what the position is for, what results it must produce, and whom it serves. Two further consequences follow. First, objectivity is the foundation of fairness: a subordinate can accept a decision about his own career only when it is clearly based on objective criteria — on what the job requires — and not on the superior's likes, dislikes or impressions; the moment a decision looks personal, trust dies. Second, objectivity is essential for the future: when the job is defined by the person, nobody knows what it really is, and when that person leaves, the business is stuck, because the job's true content goes with him or her. The objective job has a life of its own: it can be filled by the next person, and by the one after, without being redesigned each time. Jobs that are objective also make it possible to compare candidates honestly — the question is who best meets the demands of the job, not who is most like us. Integrate: write a one-page role objective for every position in BirichiNex Frameworks — purpose, results, and whom it serves — before hiring or promoting into it.

Never invent a role around a favourite employee's skills.
Judge by what the job requires, not by likeability.
Keep jobs objective so they survive the person who fills them.
State the objective criteria to the candidate before the interview.
When a job keeps failing, redefine the job — not just the person.
examples: A Kampala shopkeeper wanted to 'create a role' for her nephew. Instead, she wrote the objective first: results the new position had to produce — 20% growth in repeat customers within a year. The nephew got the job, understood the target, and delivered it — and the owner's other staff accepted the promotion without resentment.

topic: The Effective Executive — The Rules for Staffing Decisions
subtopic: Think through what the job requires, consider several people, and keep an inventory of strengths
content: There is only one right way to make a staffing decision, and it is a discipline of five steps. First, think through the assignment: what is the job, and what does it require? The job that defeated two or three good men in succession is probably wrong and must be redesigned — Drucker gives the university presidency and the international vice-presidency as classic impossible jobs. Second, consider at least several qualified people, not just the obvious one. Third, look for the man's strength — and place him where that strength produces results, because no one is strong in all areas. Fourth, discuss the decision with colleagues — two or three experienced people reviewing a candidate together see more than one executive alone. Fifth, write down the decision and the reasons, and review it after a year: the follow-up is the difference between a decision and a hope. The effective executive also keeps a running inventory of the strengths of the people around him, updated as people's capacities grow and change, so that when a position opens he can fill it from strength he already knows rather than from an advertisement. He knows that a staffing decision is a risk — the first name that comes to mind is usually the wrong name, and the decision should be retraced — and that the key test is not "Can this person do the job?" but "Can this person do this job so well that the organization is stronger for it?" Place people where their known strengths produce results.

Write the decision down and revisit it in a year.
Keep a living inventory of the strengths around you.

Eighteen months later the manager was still there and shrinkage had halved.

topic: The Effective Executive — Appraisal That Reveals Strengths
subtopic: Judge performance against expected contribution, not against potential or personality
content: The purpose of appraisal is not to judge people but to place them where their strengths can produce results — and that requires measuring performance against expected contribution, not against potential, charm or personality. Drucker's test of appraisal is severe: the appraisal system is sound only if it leads to action — the one who appraises must sit down with the person appraised and ask, "What do we expect of you in this job? What have you done well? Where could you do better?" — and the conversation must be honest and specific. The effective executive appraises against a small number of clear criteria: what the person is expected to contribute to the results of the business, and how that contribution will be known. He does not grade people on a report card of personal traits, because that measures the man rather than the performance, and it breeds fear and conformity. The effective manager asks of each person: "What did you set out to do? What did you accomplish? What did you learn?" and takes the answers seriously, because people are the one resource that can grow — and they grow to the level of the demands made on them. Appraisal is also the manager's own mirror: over time, the record of who succeeds and who fails in each position tells the manager which of his own decisions are sound and where his judgement goes wrong. Finally, appraisal protects the person: it is cruel to let someone work for years at a job that is wrong for him, and fair appraisal that reveals his strength in time lets him be placed where he can succeed. Integrate: hold a quarterly review per employee in BirichiNex CRM against the expected contribution you wrote when the role was defined, and record the strengths revealed.
tips: Appraise against expected contribution, not against personality.
Keep the criteria few, clear and known in advance.
Turn every appraisal into a two-way conversation, not a verdict.
Use appraisal to place people in strength, not to file a report.
Ask what the person learned and where the job fits them.
Review your own decisions through the record of who succeeds.
examples: A Nairobi manager gave her assistant a six-month review against the one thing they had agreed: cut payment errors by half. The assistant had exceeded it and shown a gift for reconciliation, so the manager moved her to accounts and promoted a strong seller to her role. Both thrived — while a vague 'good job, keep it up' review would have told them nothing.

topic: The Effective Executive — First Things First
subtopic: Concentrate on a few major areas; do first things first and second things not at all
content: There is always more to do than anyone can get done, so the effective executive concentrates on a few major areas where superior performance will produce outstanding results — and does first things first. The effective executive is, above all, a concentrator: one thing at a time, the thing most important right now. This is the opposite of the common plea for the "balanced executive" who is good at everything, which is a recipe for being good at nothing. Drucker quotes the old saying that the "great majority of important tasks in the world" have been done by people who did not attempt very much and did not attempt anything in a hurry. Priority demands a decision, and the decision must be made in terms of consequences: what matters most is not doing many things but doing the right things — the tasks that, if done well, will make everything else easy or unnecessary. There are always more urgent things than important things, and the effective executive resists the tyranny of the urgent: he sets priorities and sticks to them, reviews them periodically, and refuses to let the urgent crowd out the important. He also knows that second things must not be done at all — not merely done later — if the first thing is to get the full force of his attention. Concentration has a discipline: courage to say no; freedom to postpone without guilt; and the patience to finish one thing before starting another. He set aside Tuesday mornings for it alone, and paid a part-timer to run the daily reorders. Repeat revenue rose 30% in a quarter, and the small tasks had not collapsed in his absence.

topic: The Effective Executive — The Practices That Make Effectiveness
subtopic: Effectiveness is learned habits: manage time, contribute, build on strength, concentrate, decide
content: Effectiveness is not a gift people are born with; it is a discipline that can be learned — a set of practices to be acquired, one by one, until they become second nature. Drucker distills the book into five practices, each simple in statement and hard in execution. First, the effective executive knows where his time goes: he records his time, manages the unproductive demands on it, and consolidates the discretionary time left into large, unbroken blocks. Second, he focuses outward on contribution: he asks what results his organization needs and what he can contribute, and directs his work toward the outside, where results are. Third, he builds on strengths — his own, his superiors', his colleagues' and his subordinates' — and makes weaknesses irrelevant rather than the starting point. Fourth, he concentrates on the few major areas where superior performance produces outstanding results, doing first things first and second things not at all. Fifth, he makes effective decisions: he knows when a decision is needed, treats it as a matter of principle rather than of expediency, considers the alternatives, and follows through so the decision becomes action. These five practices are the whole of the effective executive's discipline — there is no sixth. They are acquired the way the musician acquires scales: by practice, repetition and self-criticism until they become automatic. Do first things first; do not do second things.

A year later his hours were down, his margin up, and two staff were running whole routines he used to touch daily.

topic: The Effective Executive — Managing the Boss
subtopic: Make your superior's strengths productive instead of trying to reform them
content: "I have no trouble managing subordinates — but how do I manage my boss?" is the question Drucker heard everywhere, and the answer is remarkably simple: make the strengths of the boss productive. Few subordinates rise over the prostrate bodies of incompetent bosses; if your boss is not promoted you stay bottled up behind them, and a replaced boss is usually followed by an outsider who brings their own team. Beyond prudence, making the boss effective lets your contribution find receptivity upstairs — it is how you accomplish the things you believe in. You do it not by toadying but by starting out with what is right and presenting it in a form the superior can actually absorb. Accept that the boss is human, with strengths and limitations and a preferred way of working. Is the boss a reader or a listener? Talking to a reader is wasted; handing a thick report to a listener is wasted. Does the boss need a one-page summary, sixty pages of figures, early involvement, or nothing until it is ripe? Adapt the "how", never the "what": put the political angle first for a politically-minded boss, the financial case first for a finance-minded one. Never try to reform the boss or tutor them out of their limitations — that is the surest way to make your own work irrelevant. Instead ask: "What can my boss do really well? What does he need to know or get from me to use his strength?" Then feed exactly that. For an employee or junior partner this is the single biggest lever on your own effectiveness: give the boss what they need to use their strength, in the shape they need it, and your contribution gets used instead of ignored. Integrate: keep your results in BirichiNex Analytics and prepare the review in your boss's preferred form — a one-pager for readers, a short walkthrough for listeners — so proof replaces persuasion.
tips: Ask what your boss can do really well, then feed that strength.
Learn whether your boss is a reader or a listener; match it.
Present the 'how' to fit the boss's style; never change the 'what'.
Stop trying to reform your boss's limitations — work around them.
Give the boss the information they need to support your idea.
A successful, promoted boss is the best promotion for you.
examples: A shop supervisor in Dar es Salaam reported to an owner who never read written memos. He switched to a five-minute verbal update with one recommendation each morning. Six months later the owner approved three of his improvement ideas — things that had sat ignored on paper for a year.

topic: The Effective Executive — Making Yourself Effective
subtopic: Know how you work best and lead from your own strengths
content: Most executives can list everything they cannot do: the boss won't let me, the government won't let me, company policy won't let me. Effective executives are equally aware of limits, but they start from the question "what can I do?" — and are astonished at how much becomes possible. The claim that somebody else won't let you do anything should always be suspected as a cover-up for inertia; even where the situation genuinely sets limits, there are usually important things that can be done, and the effective executive does them while others complain. Effectiveness also means knowing yourself as precisely as you know whether you are right- or left-handed. Do you work best in the morning or at night? Draft quickly or polish line by line? Speak from a prepared text or from notes? Work well on committees or only alone? Need pressure or a long lead time? These are not superficial — they mirror temperament, and temperament is a big factor in accomplishment. The effective executive builds on what he knows he can do and does it the way he works best. Look at your own performance and results and ask: "What do I do with relative ease that comes hard to others?" That is your comparative advantage — run the business toward it. And remember that the standard of any group is set by the performance of its leaders: raise one leader's performance and the whole average rises. Put your strongest person in the pace-setting role, feed the opportunities, and starve the problems — nowhere more than with people, starting with yourself. "What can this man do?" practised as a discipline soon becomes an attitude, and eventually you learn to ask it of yourself. topic: The Effective Executive — Sloughing Off Yesterday
subtopic: Abandon what no longer produces; drop the old before you start the new
content: Executives are forever bailing out the past — today's problems are yesterday's decisions, and yesterday's successes linger long past their productive life. The first rule of concentration is to slough off the past that has ceased to be productive. Effective executives periodically review every activity and ask: "If we were not already doing this, would we go into it now?" Unless the answer is an unconditional yes, they drop it or curtail it sharply — and they pull their best people out of the no-longer-productive past and put them to work on the opportunities of tomorrow. Total failures liquidate themselves; everyone can drop those. The dangerous ones are yesterday's successes and the "investments in managerial ego" — projects that should work and do not, which drain the lifeblood of the business because the most capable people keep pouring effort into recovering what is already sunk. Above all, slough off an old activity before starting a new one. Nothing new is easy; it always gets into trouble. The only effective way to bail out the new is with proven performers, and proven performers are always busy — you must free one before the new work can start. For a small trader this is brutally practical: the product line that has not sold in two seasons, the stall that loses money, the supplier who is always late — each is a program to put on trial for its life. Ask the question every quarter: would we start this today? If not, stop investing in it. The business that abandons products before they decline is the one too busy selling new things to need creativity seminars. Integrate: review your product and service list against BirichiNex Analytics — sales, margin, stock days — and let the data decide what earns its shelf space.

He cleared it, freed the cash, and doubled the fast-moving fittings range — total margin up 18% the following quarter.

topic: The Effective Executive — Priorities and Posteriorities
subtopic: Setting priorities is easy; the courage is in choosing what NOT to do
content: There are always more tasks than time, so a decision must be made about which deserve priority. The only question is who decides — the executive or the pressures. If the pressures decide, the important tasks are predictably sacrificed, because pressure always favours yesterday, the crisis over the opportunity, the visible over the real, the urgent over the relevant. Setting priorities is easy; everybody can do it. The difficulty is setting posteriorities — deciding what not to tackle — and sticking to the decision. What you postpone you usually abandon, and the timing is almost always wrong when you come back to it. Yet refusing to postpone anything is also a trap: doing "a little bit" of everything makes everybody happy and gets nothing done. Every posteriority is somebody else's top priority, which is exactly why the decision feels dangerous. The truly important rules are matters of courage, not analysis: pick the future as against the past; focus on opportunity rather than on problem; choose your own direction rather than climb on the bandwagon; aim high, at something that will make a difference, rather than at something safe and easy. It is as risky and as hard to do something small and new as something big and new — so make the new thing count. Achievers pick their projects by opportunity and treat other criteria as qualifiers, not determinants. Finally, never commit beyond the one task you are concentrating on now; when it is done, review the situation and pick the next task that now comes first. Concentration is the courage to impose your own judgment on time and events instead of being their whipping boy. Integrate: choose this quarter's one priority and an explicit not-doing list in BirichiNex Routines, and let Analytics confirm whether the bet paid off.
tips: Decide priorities yourself; if pressure decides, the important work loses.

Pick the future over the past, opportunity over problem.

He made 'fix supplier reliability' his one priority and openly deprioritised recruiting new customers for the quarter. On-time transport rose from 70% to 92%, and retained customers grew — a better result than chasing new ones had ever produced.

topic: The Effective Executive — Generic or Exceptional Decisions
subtopic: First decide what kind of problem you face; most problems are generic
content: Effective executives do not make many decisions; they make the few important ones well. The first question of any decision: "Is this a generic situation or an exception?" There are four kinds. One, the truly generic, where the individual event is only a symptom — most of the problems that reach your desk are of this kind, and they must be solved with a rule, a policy, a principle. Two, the problem that is unique for your business but generic in the world — the first big cross-border order, the first hire — where you must borrow rules from others' experience. Three, the truly exceptional and unique, which is rare and must be handled case by case. Four, the early manifestation of a new generic problem — what looks like a one-off may be the first sign of something that will recur. Classifying wrongly is the most common error. The biggest mistake is treating a generic situation as a series of unique events — patching symptoms pragmatically when a principle is needed; this produces endless frustration and futility. Almost as common is treating a new event as another example of an old problem and applying rules that no longer fit. The effective decision-maker therefore always assumes initially that the problem is generic, looks past the symptom for the true problem, and pushes the solution to the highest conceptual level — a rule that turns every future occurrence into a case under the rule. "A country with many laws is a country of incompetent lawyers": an executive who makes many decisions is lazy and ineffectual. A trader's version: one late supplier is an event; a pattern of late suppliers is a generic problem demanding a sourcing policy. Integrate: log recurring problems in BirichiNex CRM and Analytics; when the same issue appears three times, it is generic — time to write a policy instead of another patch.
tips: Ask first: is this a one-off, a symptom, or a new pattern?
Assume generic until proven exceptional.
Solve generic problems with a rule, not another patch.
