Fix the true problem, not the symptom it wears.
One good policy should end a whole family of decisions.
examples: An importer in Mombasa kept refunding customers for crushed goods, treating each as a unique claim. When he logged them he found one cause: a fragile crate design. He wrote a packaging specification for all suppliers, and claims fell 90% within a quarter.

topic: The Effective Executive — Define the Boundary Conditions
subtopic: Decide what the decision must accomplish before you choose
content: The second element of an effective decision is clear specifications: what objectives must the decision reach, what minimum goals must it attain, what conditions must it satisfy? Drucker calls these the boundary conditions — the specifications any acceptable solution has to meet. The more concisely and clearly they are stated, the more likely the decision will actually work. A serious shortfall in defining them makes a decision ineffectual no matter how brilliant it looks. Ask: "What is the minimum needed to resolve this problem?" Sloan kept autonomy and responsibility in the operating divisions as a boundary condition of his General Motors structure — so the answer had to be constitutional, not a personality fix. Boundary conditions also tell you when to abandon a decision. The Schlieffen Plan failed because his successors forgot its core commitment — never split the German forces — and kept the plan while making its attainment impossible. Roosevelt succeeded because when the boundary conditions changed (economic recovery became political survival) he abandoned the old plan instantly and switched to a new one. Clear thinking about boundary conditions also exposes the most dangerous decision of all: the one that might work only if nothing whatever goes wrong — a prayer for a miracle, like the Bay of Pigs, which demanded both Castro's overthrow and no visible U.S. intervention. When the specifications are incompatible, the decision is not a decision but a wish. For a trader: before buying that container of bales, write the conditions — minimum margin, delivery date, quality grade, cash tied up. If a plan needs everything to go right to break even, it is not a plan. Integrate: state the boundary conditions of each big move in BirichiNex Finance and Inventory — minimum margin, maximum stock days, payback — so the AI Advisor can flag impossible specifications.
tips: Write the minimum the decision must achieve before choosing.
State boundary conditions concisely — clarity improves the odds.
When conditions change, abandon the old plan without sentiment.
Flag any decision that needs a miracle to work — then change it.
Check that your specifications are compatible, not contradictory.
The clearer the specs, the easier the final choice.
examples: A trader in Kigali wanted to stock a new phone brand on credit from a Nairobi supplier. She wrote the boundary conditions: 30% margin, restock within 60 days, supplier holds delivery risk. The credit terms failed two of the three — she declined, and six months later the brand had still not delivered the promised margins to competitors.

topic: The Effective Executive — What Is Right, Not Who Is Right
subtopic: Think through the right answer first; only then make the compromise
content: One always has to compromise in the end — so start from what is right rather than what is acceptable, and certainly rather than who is right. If you do not know what is right, you cannot tell the right compromise from the wrong one, and you will end up making the wrong one. Sloan's instruction to the young Drucker on his first consulting study is the classic: "Put down what you think is right as you see it. Don't worry about our reaction. Don't concern yourself with the compromises. There is not one executive here who does not know how to make every conceivable compromise — but he cannot make the right compromise unless you first tell him what right is." There are two kinds of compromise. One is "half a loaf is better than no bread" — the boundary conditions are still satisfied; half a loaf is still food. The other is the Judgment of Solomon — "half a baby is worse than no baby at all"; the essential condition is destroyed, and half a baby is a corpse in two pieces. Worrying about acceptability wastes time: the objections you fear rarely happen, while obstacles nobody imagined turn out to be huge. Starting from "what is acceptable" gives away the important things and loses any chance of an effective answer. Kennedy learned this lesson from the Bay of Pigs and applied it in the missile crisis — knowing precisely which specification was non-negotiable (the missiles had to physically leave) and which could be conceded (the on-the-ground inspection). For a seller this governs everything from pricing to supplier terms: settle first, in writing, what the right deal is for your business, then negotiate from that anchor. Integrate: set your right position — minimum margin, terms, price floor — as parameters in BirichiNex Finance and let the AI Advisor keep your negotiations anchored to them.
tips: Work out the right answer before you consider what is acceptable.
Know which conditions are non-negotiable and which can bend.
Accept 'half a loaf' compromises; refuse 'half a baby' ones.
Do not start from 'what will they accept' — you lose the important things.
Anchor every negotiation on your pre-written right position.
Fear of reaction is a waste of time; the real obstacles surprise you.
examples: A supplier in Nairobi demanded a 30% discount from Amina's shop or no contract. Instead of haggling from fear, she held her right position — pay on delivery, 25% margin, quality inspection — and offered a volume compromise. The supplier conceded the payment terms; she kept her margin and walked away from a bad contract.

topic: The Effective Executive — Converting the Decision into Action
subtopic: No decision is made until someone owns the work, deadline and communication
content: The most time-consuming step in decision-making is not reaching the decision but putting it into effect. Unless a decision "degenerates into work", it is not a decision — at best a good intention. That is the trouble with so many policy statements: they contain no action commitment, so nobody treats them as real. Converting a decision into action requires answering distinct questions: Who has to know of this decision? What action has to be taken? Who is to take it? And what does the action have to be so that the people who must do it can do it? The first and last questions are the most often overlooked. Drucker's machine-tool company decided to phase out a model — and nobody informed the purchasing clerk whose order logic still bought parts for it, leaving a warehouse full of parts for a discontinued product. The action must also fit the capacities of the people who will carry it out: a chemical company launched identical businesses in two West African countries; one required scarce technical managers and had to be liquidated, while the other was designed for local staff and was sold at a profit. When a decision requires changed behaviour, you must change measurements and incentives at the same time — if the greatest rewards still go to the old behaviour, everyone concludes the old course is what the top really wants. For a trader this is the difference between "we should sell online" and "by Friday, Joseph lists twenty items and the family WhatsApp handles replies". Naming the owner, the action and the deadline is what separates a decision from a hope. Ask who else must know — the clerk who buys the parts.
Fit the action to the people available; do not design over their heads.
When behaviour must change, change the rewards and measures too.
A decision without a deadline is a hope, not a plan.

topic: The Effective Executive — Feedback: Test Decisions Against Reality
subtopic: Go and look for yourself; never trust reports alone
content: A feedback loop must be built into every decision, testing the expectations that underlie it against actual events. Men are fallible; even the best decisions eventually become obsolete, and reality never stands still for long. The military learned centuries ago that most orders are futile unless checked — that is why a battalion commander goes into the mess hall and tastes the food from the same kettle as his men. Reports are not enough; the officer who gave the order goes out and sees for himself, or sends his own aide, because communication cannot be trusted to pass back faithfully. This matters even more as computers and dashboards move decision-makers further from the scene — a computer handles abstractions, and abstractions are reliable only if constantly checked against the concrete. Failure to go and look is the typical reason people persist in a course long after it has stopped making sense. Build the feedback in from the start: what would the facts have to show for the decision to be working? Then check systematically — for people decisions, review the outcome six to nine months later; if it failed, do not blame the person, examine your own judgment. Vail's and Sloan's great decisions all had to be rethought as conditions changed; the best decisions are eventually outflanked by reality, and clear feedback is what lets you abandon or revise in time. For a trader: the decision to stock a new line carries a built-in check — sell-through after thirty days, margin after sixty. Integrate: set the check-ins in BirichiNex Analytics — margin, stock days, repeat rate — and review them on a fixed date rather than when you feel like it.
tips: Decide in advance what facts would prove the decision right.
Go and look yourself; do not rely on reports or hearsay.
Review people decisions 6–9 months later — and audit your own call.
When the check shows failure, revise or abandon; do not double down.
Check your assumptions regularly; reality never stands still.
Use live dashboards, but verify them against the shop floor.
examples: A retailer in Arusha decided a 20% promotion would clear slow stock and set the check: sell-through within 14 days. At day 12 the data showed only 6% had moved — so she stopped the promotion, changed the bundle, and cleared the stock at margin instead of at a loss.

topic: The Effective Executive — Decide Through Dissent, Not Consensus
subtopic: Start with opinions, test them, and organise disagreement
content: Most books say "first find the facts". The effective executive knows you cannot start with facts — you start with opinions, which are untested hypotheses, and you test them against reality. People experienced in an area are supposed to have opinions; asking them for facts first is undesirable, because they will simply find the facts that fit their conclusion — and everyone can find those. The rigorous method is to recognise that opinions come first, then insist that each opinion be converted into something testable: "What would the facts have to be for this opinion to hold?" "What must we look at, study and test?" Finding the right criterion of relevance — the right measurement — is usually the hinge of the whole decision. Then comes the harder rule: make decisions on the clash of conflicting views, not on consensus. Sloan once opened a meeting with "I take it we are all in complete agreement" — and proposed postponing the matter "to give ourselves time to develop disagreement". There are three reasons dissent is necessary. It is the only safeguard against becoming the prisoner of the organisation, where everyone is a special pleader wanting something from you. It provides alternatives — a decision without an alternative is a desperate gambler's throw, and when reality proves it wrong you need a fallback that has already been thought through. And disagreement stimulates imagination; argued, documented disagreement is the best stimulus we know. So the effective executive asks of a dissenter: "What does this person have to see for his position to be tenable?" — seeking understanding before deciding who is right. For a seller, this means listening hard to the customer who says the price is wrong and the supplier who says the quality is bad, then testing both claims with data. tips: Treat opinions as hypotheses and define what would test them.
Find the right measurement before you decide what counts as fact.
Do not make a decision until there is real disagreement.
Protect yourself from special pleading by seeking dissent deliberately.
Keep a thought-through alternative ready for every big decision.
Ask what the dissenter must see for their view to be rational.
examples: A wholesaler in Kampala believed slow sales meant his prices were too high. His field agent insisted the issue was delivery time. Instead of arguing, they tested both claims against sales by delivery speed. Delivery, not price, was the real driver — and fixing it raised repeat orders 20%.

topic: The Effective Executive — Is a Decision Really Necessary?
subtopic: Act when inaction makes things worse; otherwise leave well alone
content: The effective decision-maker's final question: is a decision really necessary? One alternative is always doing nothing. Every decision is like surgery — an intervention in a system that carries the risk of shock — and you do not perform unnecessary surgery. There are three situations. You must decide when a condition is likely to degenerate if nothing is done; Vail's contemporaries fought the threat of government ownership symptom by symptom, but Vail saw that winning battles while losing the war was pointless and created a radically new policy instead. You should not interfere when the condition will take care of itself — the answer to "what will happen if we do nothing?" is "it will take care of itself" — nor when the problem is annoying but unimportant. "De minimis non curat praetor" — the magistrate does not consider trifles. Most decisions lie between these extremes: the problem will not fix itself but is unlikely to turn malignant; the opportunity is real but not transformative. Here, compare the effort and risk of action against the risk of inaction, and use two guidelines: act if the benefits greatly outweigh the cost and risk; and act or do not act, but never hedge or compromise. The surgeon who removes half the tonsils risks as much as one who removes all — and cures nothing; half-action is the one thing that is always wrong. When the decision is ready, most are lost at the last step because they are unpleasant, unpopular or difficult — effective ones usually are. Do not cave to "let's make another study" unless there is reason to believe more study would produce something new and relevant. And listen to your inner daemon: if something feels off, hold a moment; if nothing surfaces in a few days, act with speed and energy. Executives are paid to get the right things done, not to do things they like.
